opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the honest answer is that Operator today is an early research preview, and you should think about it that way. It's genuinely useful for a certain class of tasks, the kind of things where you'd otherwise be clicking through a bunch of web pages, filling out forms, doing something tedious that doesn't require a ton of judgment but does take your time. Things like booking a reservation, ordering groceries, pulling together some information from a few different sites. For those, it can actually save you time, and it's kind of magical the first time you watch it work.

But it's also not reliable enough yet that you'd hand it something really high-stakes and walk away. It makes mistakes, it gets stuck on certain websites, sometimes it's slower than just doing the thing yourself. So we built it with the expectation that the user stays somewhat in the loop. It'll ask for confirmation before doing anything consequential, like submitting a payment, and you can take over the browser at any point.

The way I think about it is that this is the beginning of a trajectory. The underlying capability, a model that can actually use a computer the way a person does, by looking at the screen and clicking and typing, is really general. The current version is limited, but the reason we wanted to get it out there is that we learn a ton from seeing how people actually use it, where it breaks, what tasks they reach for. And we've seen with other model capabilities that once you have something that works some of the time, it tends to improve pretty quickly. So I'd say it's useful today for a narrow set of things, and the more exciting part is where it's going.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that Operator today is more of a preview of where things are going than something I'd tell most people to build their workflow around. And I say that as someone who's pretty bullish on the direction.

If you look at what it's actually good at right now, it's the stuff where the task is fairly well-specified, the website is reasonably well-behaved, and the cost of a mistake is low. Booking a reservation, filling out a form, comparing a few product pages. Those things mostly work, and when they work it genuinely feels a little magical, because you're watching the model navigate a browser the same way you would.

But the moment you get into anything with more ambiguity, or a site that has a weird UI, or a long multi-step task where one early mistake compounds, the reliability drops off pretty fast. And the thing about agents is that reliability is the whole game. If I have to watch it the entire time to make sure it doesn't do something dumb, then I haven't really saved any time. I've just changed what I'm doing with my hands.

So the way I'd frame it is, Operator is useful today as a research artifact and as a signal. It's useful for OpenAI, because they're collecting enormous amounts of data about where these systems fail in the real world. And it's useful for the rest of us because it tells you what the interface is going to look like and what the hard problems are. The hard problems aren't really the model being smart enough to understand the task. They're things like recovering gracefully from errors, knowing when to ask the user versus when to just proceed, and dealing with the fact that the web was not designed for this.

What I'd watch for is the same curve we saw with code generation. Two or three years ago, Copilot was neat but you couldn't trust it. Now a lot of engineers have it in the loop constantly. I think computer-use agents are at the "neat but can't trust it" stage, and the interesting question is how fast that transition happens, and whether it's driven mostly by better models or by better scaffolding around them. My bet is it's more scaffolding and evaluation than people expect.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s useful today for tasks where you can give it a clear objective, let it run for a while, and then check the result pretty easily. The question is how much supervision it needs along the way. If I have to watch every click and correct it repeatedly, then I might as well do the task myself.

So I’d distinguish between being able to demonstrate that it can do something and being reliable enough that you actually delegate that thing to it. There’s value at the current stage, particularly for bounded tasks where mistakes are easy to catch and recover from. But I think the bigger opportunity is getting to the point where you can hand it work and trust that it will either finish or come back with a useful question when it gets stuck.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s useful today, but for a fairly narrow set of tasks. There’s a difference between watching it do something impressive and trusting it to take care of something for you. If you have to watch every step and correct it along the way, you haven’t necessarily saved much time.

So the question for me is: can you give it a task, walk away, and come back to a result you can verify quickly? For some tasks, that’s already possible. But for longer workflows, small errors can compound, and reliability becomes the bottleneck. I’m excited about the direction, but I’d think of it today as something to experiment with and use selectively, with a person still checking the outcome.
